question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Be my guest
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Please do it.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Be my guest" means used to give someone permission to do something, or to invite them to go ahead and do as they wish. (जी हाँ ज़रूर करें/आपकी मर्ज़ी)
◦ Example: "Can I use your phone?" "Be my guest."

• It is a polite, informal way of granting permission or encouraging someone to proceed with an action without hesitation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Stop, don't go ahead: This is the opposite meaning of the idiom; "Be my guest" never conveys refusal or a warning to stop.

• Option 3: Be with me: This is a literal, unrelated meaning and does not capture the sense of granting permission.

• Option 4: Come with me: This confuses "guest" with an invitation to accompany someone, which is not what the idiom conveys.

NOTE

• Other common permission-related idioms/expressions used in SSC exams: "Feel free to", "Go ahead", and "By all means" — all used to grant permission readily.

question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, then select the option "No error".
And, indeed, there was/ hardly picture in Rome I was unable/ to reattribute to its rightful owner.
option_1: to reattribute to its rightful owner.
option_4: hardly picture in Rome I was unable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. hardly picture in Rome I was unable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "hardly picture in Rome I was unable" is missing the indefinite article "a" before the noun "picture". The correct phrasing should be "hardly a picture in Rome I was unable".

• Rule — Use of Articles: A singular countable noun (like "picture") must always be preceded by an article (a/an/the) or another determiner when used in a general, non-specific sense.

• Corrected sentence: "And, indeed, there was hardly a picture in Rome I was unable to reattribute to its rightful owner."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to reattribute to its rightful owner." is grammatically correct as the infinitive phrase completing the sentence; it contains no error.

• Option 2: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist in the sentence (the missing article), so this option cannot be chosen.

• Option 3: "And, indeed, there was" is grammatically correct; it is a simple introductory clause with correct subject-verb agreement.

NOTE

• Missing/incorrect use of articles (a/an/the) is one of the most frequently tested error types in SSC error-spotting questions.

• Remember: "hardly" is an adverb of degree and does not affect the need for an article before a following singular countable noun.

question:
Choose the option that is the correct indirect form of the sentence.
She said, “I will be available tomorrow.”
option_1: She said that she would be available tomorrow.
option_2: She said that she would be available the next day.
option_3: She said that she must be available the next day.
option_4: She said that she will be available the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. She said that she would be available the next day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The reported speech contains the modal "will", a first-person subject "I", and the time expression "tomorrow".

• Rule — Narration change:
◦ Modal "will" changes to "would" in indirect speech when the reporting verb is in the past tense ("said").
◦ The time expression "tomorrow" changes to "the next day".
◦ The pronoun "I" changes to "she" to match the subject of the reporting verb.

• Applying the rule: "I will be available tomorrow" → "she would be available the next day."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because the time expression "tomorrow" has not been changed to "the next day", even though the reporting verb is in the past tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because the modal has been wrongly changed to "must", which alters the original meaning of simple futurity expressed by "will".

• Option 4 is incorrect because the modal "will" has not been changed to "would", which is required since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense.

NOTE

• Common time-expression changes in narration: today → that day; tomorrow → the next day/the following day; yesterday → the day before/the previous day; now → then; here → there; this → that.

• Common modal changes: will → would; can → could; may → might; shall → should (in first person).

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
Belonging to the same kind
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Homogeneous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Homogeneous" means of the same kind; consisting of parts or elements that are all of the same type. (समान प्रकार का/सजातीय)
◦ Example: The class was a homogeneous group of students, all from the same background.

• The word is formed from the Greek roots "homo-" (same) + "genos" (kind/race), literally meaning "of the same kind."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sebaceous" (वसामय): relating to oil or fat, especially as secreted by sebaceous glands in the skin; unrelated to "same kind".

• Option 2: "Heterogeneous" (विविध प्रकार का): consisting of dissimilar or diverse elements; this is the exact opposite of the required meaning.

• Option 4: "Casserole" (एक बर्तन विशेष): a large, deep dish used for cooking and serving food; a completely unrelated word.

NOTE

• Commonly confused opposite pair in SSC vocabulary: Homogeneous (same kind) ↔ Heterogeneous (different kinds).

• Related one-word substitutions: Synonymous (having the same meaning), Congruent (in agreement/matching).

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
BOGUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. FALSE.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bogus" means not genuine or true; fake; fraudulent. (जाली/नकली)
◦ Example: He was arrested for using a bogus passport.

• Since "false" also means not genuine or real, it is the closest synonym among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "HUMANE" (दयालु): showing compassion or kindness; unrelated in meaning to "bogus".

• Option 2: "STRONG" (मजबूत): having great physical power or force; unrelated in meaning to "bogus".

• Option 4: "CRITICIZE" (आलोचना करना): to express disapproval of someone or something; unrelated in meaning to "bogus".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "bogus": fake, sham, counterfeit, spurious, fraudulent, phony.

• Antonym of "bogus": genuine, authentic, real.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. MALODOROUS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Malodorous" — having an unpleasant or offensive smell.
◦ Example: The malodorous garbage dump was a source of constant complaints from residents.

• Spelling key: MAL + ODOROUS, from the Latin prefix "mal-" (bad) and "odor" (smell), meaning literally "bad-smelling".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "HEIRARCHY" — incorrect; the correct spelling is "Hierarchy" (the "e" and "i" are reversed).

• Option 2: "APPAULLING" — incorrect; the correct spelling is "Appalling" (correct form has one "p" and double "l": a-p-p-a-l-l-i-n-g).

• Option 3: "PESTILLENTIAL" — incorrect; the correct spelling is "Pestilential" (only a single "l" appears before "ential").

NOTE

• Frequently misspelt words tested by SSC: hierarchy, appalling, pestilential, entrepreneur, questionnaire, embarrass, occurrence, accommodate.

• Tip: words ending in "-ous" (like malodorous, hazardous, dangerous) rarely double their consonants before the suffix.

question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given group of words.
A person who is experiencing dementia brought about by old age
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Senile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Senile" means showing a loss of mental faculties, especially memory, associated with old age; suffering from dementia due to old age. (बुढ़ापे के कारण मानसिक दुर्बलता से ग्रस्त)
◦ Example: Her grandfather had become senile and often forgot the names of his own children.

• The word derives from the Latin "senex", meaning "old man" — the same root as words like "senior" and "senate".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Sentinel" (प्रहरी): a soldier or guard whose job is to stand and keep watch; unrelated to old age or dementia.

• Option 3: "Primal" (आदिम/मूल): of first importance; fundamental or original; unrelated to the given meaning.

• Option 4: "Primitive" (आदिम): relating to an early stage of development, simple or basic; unrelated to old-age dementia.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Amnesia (loss of memory), Dotage (the period of old age marked by weakened mental faculties), Geriatric (relating to old people, especially medical care of the elderly).

question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below
Polarize
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Combine.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Polarize" means to divide or cause people to divide into two sharply contrasting groups or sets of opinions or beliefs. (दो विरोधी गुटों में बांटना)
◦ Example: The issue has polarized public opinion, with people taking strongly opposing sides.

• Since "polarize" means to separate into opposing camps, its antonym must express the idea of bringing together/uniting, which is exactly what "combine" means: to join or merge two or more things into one. (मिलाना/एकजुट करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Orchestrate" (आयोजित करना): to plan or coordinate the elements of a situation carefully to achieve a desired effect; it is neither a synonym nor a true antonym of "polarize".

• Option 3: "Conjoin" (संयुक्त करना): to join or link together; while close in sense to "combine", it is a rarer, more formal word (typically used for physical joining, e.g. "conjoined twins") and is not as natural a fit as the everyday word "combine".

• Option 4: "Segregate" is incorrect as an antonym — it means to separate or set apart from the rest, which is actually close in meaning to "polarize" (both describe dividing into separate groups), not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested by SSC around this theme: Unite ↔ Divide, Merge ↔ Separate, Converge ↔ Diverge, Integrate ↔ Segregate.

• Do not confuse "antonym" questions with "synonym" questions — always check whether the given word and the chosen option express opposite or similar ideas before marking the answer.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. TREBBLE.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "TREBBLE" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "Treble" — meaning three times as much or as many; triple.
◦ Example: His salary was trebled after the promotion.

• Spelling key: TREBLE has only a single "b", unlike "TREBBLE" which wrongly doubles it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "SUPPORT" is correctly spelt — to give assistance or approval.

• Option 2: "TUNNEL" is correctly spelt — an underground passage.

• Option 3: "RAPPORT" is correctly spelt — a close and harmonious relationship.

NOTE

• Words that are often wrongly given a double consonant by test-takers: treble, benefit, develop, until, profited, focused.

• Double-consonant rule: a consonant is usually doubled before a suffix only when the preceding syllable is stressed and ends in a single vowel + single consonant (e.g., "occur" → "occurred").

question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given group of words.
Dependent on chance or uncertainty
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Precarious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Precarious" means dependent on chance or uncertain circumstances; not securely held or in position; likely to fall or collapse. (अनिश्चित/जोखिम भरा)
◦ Example: The refugees were living in precarious conditions, unsure of their future.

• The word comes from the Latin "precarius", meaning "obtained by entreaty/depending on the favour of another", reflecting the sense of instability and uncertainty.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Paradox" (विरोधाभास): a statement or situation that seems self-contradictory but may be true; unrelated to uncertainty/chance.

• Option 3: "Presume" (मान लेना): to suppose that something is true without proof; a verb, not matching the given meaning.

• Option 4: "Presumptuous" (अहंकारी/धृष्ट): failing to observe the limits of what is permitted or appropriate; overconfident or bold; unrelated to the given meaning.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Precarious" with the similarly-spelt but unrelated "Presume/Presumptuous", which come from a different root ("praesumere", to take beforehand).

• Related word: "Precariousness" (noun form) — the state of being uncertain or risky.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Our study goes
P. beyond LDL cholesterol levels to get
Q. and the impact of eating walnuts daily
R. a complete picture of all of the lipoproteins
S. on their potential to improve cardiovascular risk
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. PRQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must logically flow: "Our study goes" + P + R + Q + S.

• Reconstructed sentence: "Our study goes beyond LDL cholesterol levels to get [P] a complete picture of all of the lipoproteins [R] and the impact of eating walnuts daily [Q] on their potential to improve cardiovascular risk [S]."

• Logic: P introduces the purpose ("to get a complete picture"); R immediately supplies the object of "get" ("a complete picture of all of the lipoproteins"); Q then adds a second, parallel object joined by "and" ("the impact of eating walnuts daily"); S finally supplies the common qualifying phrase ("on their potential to improve cardiovascular risk") that applies to both R and Q.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (SRPQ) is incorrect because it places S immediately after the opening stem, breaking the logical link between "to get" (end of P) and "a complete picture" (start of R).

• Option 2 (PQSR) is incorrect because it places Q (which depends on R via "and") before R, so "and the impact..." has nothing to connect to.

• Option 4 (SPQR) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 1 — S cannot follow the stem directly since it needs to complete the P-R-Q chain at the end.

NOTE

• In para/sentence-rearrangement questions, always locate the segment that logically completes the verb/infinitive in the opening stem (here, "goes ... to get") before evaluating the rest.

• Look for connector words like "and" — they signal that the segment they begin must follow a parallel, already-introduced idea.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Buy a lemon
option_1: To buy something that is of much less value.
option_3: To work through the day and shop in the evening
option_4: To give importance to little things
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To buy something that is of much less value.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Buy a lemon" means to purchase something, especially a vehicle, that turns out to be defective or of much less value than what was paid for it. (ऐसी चीज़ खरीदना जो घटिया/दोषपूर्ण निकले)
◦ Example: He bought a lemon when he purchased that old car — it broke down within a week.

• The idiom originates from American slang, where a "lemon" refers to a faulty product (particularly a car), linking the sourness of the fruit to the unpleasant experience of getting a bad deal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: To lose foundation: an unrelated, made-up meaning with no connection to the idiom.

• Option 3: To work through the day and shop in the evening: describes an unrelated daily routine, not the idiom's meaning.

• Option 4: To give importance to little things: this describes a different idea altogether, not "buy a lemon".

NOTE

• Other consumer/deal-related idioms tested by SSC: "A good bargain" (a favourable deal), "To pay through the nose" (to pay too much for something), "Daylight robbery" (being charged an unfairly high price).

question:
Select the option that will improve the bracketed part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select ‘No improvement’.
He spent many an hours playing the chess across the city.
option_2: He have spent many an hours playing the chess across the
option_3: He had spent many an hours playing the chess across the
option_4: He spent many an hour playing the chess across the
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He spent many an hour playing the chess across the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence wrongly uses the plural noun "hours" after the structure "many a", giving "many an hours".

• Rule — "Many a" + Singular Noun: The expression "many a" is always followed by a singular countable noun and takes a singular verb, even though the meaning is plural (e.g., "many a man has failed" — not "many a men have failed").

• Applying the rule: "many an hours" must be corrected to "many an hour" (the article changes to "an" before the vowel sound of "hour", and the noun stays singular).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No improvement" is incorrect because the sentence does contain an error — the plural "hours" after "many a" is ungrammatical.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it changes "spent" to the ungrammatical "have spent" without a corresponding subject-verb structure, and it also fails to correct "an hours" to "an hour".

• Option 3 is incorrect because although "had spent" is grammatically possible in some contexts, it unnecessarily changes the tense of the original sentence, and it still fails to correct "an hours" to "an hour".

NOTE

• Similar constructions frequently tested by SSC: "many a time", "many a day", "many a book" — always singular noun + singular verb.

• Do not confuse "many a + singular noun" with "many + plural noun" (e.g., "many hours", "many books"), which is also correct but a different structure.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Desiccate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Hydrate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Desiccate" means to remove the moisture from something; to dry out thoroughly. (सुखाना/निर्जलीकरण करना)
◦ Example: The fruit was desiccated in the sun to preserve it for winter.

• "Hydrate" means to cause to absorb water; to add moisture to, which is the direct opposite of removing moisture.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Honour" (सम्मान करना): to regard or treat someone with great respect; unrelated to moisture.

• Option 2: "Ascend" (चढ़ना): to rise or climb upward; unrelated to moisture or drying.

• Option 4: "Venerate" (आदर करना): to regard with great respect or reverence; unrelated to moisture.

NOTE

• Related word pairs: Desiccate ↔ Moisten/Hydrate/Soak; Dehydrate ↔ Hydrate.

• The prefix "de-" in "desiccate/dehydrate" often signals removal or reduction, useful for quickly identifying antonym pairs involving moisture.

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
Such was the education / of the Spartans with regard to / one of the greatest of there kings.
option_2: one of the greatest of there kings.
option_4: of the Spartans with regard to
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. one of the greatest of there kings.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "one of the greatest of there kings" wrongly uses "there" (an adverb of place) instead of "their" (a possessive pronoun/adjective).

• Rule — There vs. Their: "There" refers to a place or is used as an introductory word (e.g., "there is/are"), while "their" is a possessive form showing ownership, used before a noun (here, "kings").

• Corrected segment: "one of the greatest of their kings."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist in the sentence (the "there/their" confusion).

• Option 3: "Such was the education" is grammatically correct; it is a properly inverted introductory clause.

• Option 4: "of the Spartans with regard to" is grammatically correct; the phrase "with regard to" is correctly used.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophones frequently tested by SSC: there/their/they're, its/it's, your/you're, whose/who's.

• Memory tip: "their" contains the word "heir", which relates to possession/ownership, helping distinguish it from "there" (place).

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Sane
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Paranoid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Sane" means of sound mind; rational and sensible; not mad or mentally ill. (स्वस्थ मस्तिष्क वाला/समझदार)
◦ Example: Despite the pressure, she remained calm and sane throughout the ordeal.

• "Paranoid" means exhibiting irrational suspicion or mistrust of others; suffering from delusions, which directly contrasts with being mentally sound and rational.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Reposeful" (शांत): calm, restful, relaxed; this is close in spirit to "sane" (composed), not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Stoical" (धैर्यवान): enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining; not an opposite of "sane".

• Option 4: "Halcyon" (शांतिपूर्ण): denoting a period of time that was peaceful and happy; unrelated to mental soundness, not an opposite of "sane".

NOTE

• Other antonym pairs of "sane": Sane ↔ Insane, Deranged, Demented, Lunatic.

• Do not confuse antonym questions with questions asking for words of similar temperament — "reposeful", "stoical" and "halcyon" all describe calmness, which is closer in spirit to "sane" than opposite to it.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
His shoes were soaked from walk through the dew.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. soaked from walking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined portion "soaked from walk" wrongly uses the bare verb "walk" after the preposition "from".

• Rule — Preposition + Gerund: A preposition (such as "from", "of", "in", "on", "after", "before") must always be followed by a gerund (verb + -ing), not the base form of the verb.

• Applying the rule: "from walk" must be corrected to "from walking", giving "His shoes were soaked from walking through the dew."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "soak from walking" is incorrect because it wrongly changes the passive participle "soaked" to the base verb "soak", breaking the passive construction "were soaked".

• Option 3: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain an error — the bare verb "walk" cannot follow the preposition "from".

• Option 4: "soaks from walk" is incorrect because it wrongly changes "soaked" to the present-tense "soaks" (which doesn't agree with the past tense "were") and also fails to convert "walk" into the required gerund form.

NOTE

• The "preposition + gerund" rule is one of the most frequently tested grammar rules in SSC exams: e.g., "good at swimming", "tired of waiting", "interested in learning".

• Do not confuse a gerund (verb+ing used as a noun) with a present participle used in continuous tenses — both have the same "-ing" form but different grammatical roles.

question:
Choose the option that is the correct passive form of the sentence.
We had eaten the cake.
option_1: The cake had been eaten by us.
option_2: The cake will be eaten by us.
option_3: The cake is eaten by us.
option_4: The cake was eaten by us.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The cake had been eaten by us.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "We had eaten the cake" is in the Past Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + had + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + had been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the cake" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "had been" is used; the verb "eaten" (V3 of "eat") is retained; and "we" becomes the agent with "by us".
◦ Passive: The cake had been eaten by us.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "will be eaten" is the passive form of the Simple Future Tense, not the Past Perfect Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is eaten" is the passive form of the Simple Present Tense, not the Past Perfect Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was eaten" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Past Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• Tense-wise passive auxiliary chart: Simple Present → is/am/are + V3; Simple Past → was/were + V3; Simple Future → will be + V3; Present Perfect → has/have been + V3; Past Perfect → had been + V3.

• The past participle (V3) form always remains the same across all these passive structures — only the auxiliary changes according to tense.

question:
Some parts of a few sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
I didn’t speak to the sage again for many years,
A. seer, born on a dark island of a union between an ascetic and a fisher princess
B. because of the many hefty books, he’d written. Vyasa the
C. though I heard of him from time to time. I learned
D. his name: Vyasa the Compendious,
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. CDBA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct sequence is C-D-B-A, forming: "I didn't speak to the sage again for many years, though I heard of him from time to time. I learned [C] his name: Vyasa the Compendious, [D] because of the many hefty books, he'd written. Vyasa the [B] seer, born on a dark island of a union between an ascetic and a fisher princess [A]."

• Logic: C follows the opening stem naturally with the concessive clause "though I heard of him..."; D then supplies what "I learned" — his name; B explains how the name was learned ("because of the many hefty books he'd written") and reintroduces "Vyasa the..."; A finally completes the description begun by B ("Vyasa the seer, born on...").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ABCD) is incorrect because it begins with A, which is a continuation of a description ("seer, born on...") that has no antecedent yet — nothing has introduced "Vyasa" at that point.

• Option 2 (DCAB) is incorrect because it places D right after the stem, but the stem's clause ("though I heard of him... I learned") must come before "his name" is revealed in D.

• Option 4 (BADC) is incorrect because it starts with B, which references "the many hefty books he'd written" without first establishing who "he" is or that a name was learned.

NOTE

• In jumbled-sentence questions, locate the segment that grammatically and logically continues the opening stem first, then trace pronoun/name references (e.g., "his name", "Vyasa the...") to link the remaining parts in sequence.

• Watch for repeated words/phrases (here, "Vyasa the" appears at the end of segment D and again at the end of segment B) — they are strong clues to correct sequencing.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A leader who sways his followers by his oratory
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Demagogue.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Demagogue" means a political leader who seeks support by appealing to the desires and prejudices of ordinary people rather than by rational argument; a leader who sways followers through powerful oratory. (लोकरंजक नेता)
◦ Example: The demagogue whipped up the crowd's emotions with an impassioned speech.

• The word comes from the Greek "demos" (people) + "agogos" (leading), literally meaning "leader of the people".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Fugitive" (भगोड़ा): a person who has escaped from custody or is in hiding; unrelated to leadership or oratory.

• Option 2: "Narcissist" (आत्ममुग्ध व्यक्ति): a person who has an excessive interest in or admiration of themselves; unrelated to swaying followers through speech.

• Option 3: "Impostor" (धोखेबाज़): a person who pretends to be someone else to deceive others; unrelated to the given meaning.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions: Orator (a skilled public speaker), Rhetorician (one skilled in the art of persuasive speaking), Autocrat (a ruler with absolute power).

• Do not confuse "demagogue" (manipulative leader) with "diplomat" (a tactful negotiator) — a common distractor pairing in SSC papers.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

I would uncover the story that lay (1) ______ between the lines of the men's exploits. Better still, I (2) ______ one of them tell it herself, with all her joys and doubts, her struggles and her triumphs, her heartbreaks, her achievements, the unique female way (3) ______ which she sees her world and her place in it. And who could be (4) ______ for this than Panchaali? It is her life, her voice, her questions, and her vision that I invite you (5) ______ 'The Palace of Illusions'.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. invisible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "I would uncover the story that lay invisible between the lines of the men's exploits."

• The verb "uncover" means to reveal something that was hidden or not visible. Since the author speaks of "uncovering" the story, the story must have been invisible (unseen) between the lines before being uncovered.

• Rule — Contextual/Collocation fit: The chosen word must logically pair with the surrounding verb and sense of the sentence; here "uncover ... that lay invisible" forms a coherent cause-effect relationship (something hidden needs to be revealed).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "visible" is incorrect because it contradicts the idea of "uncovering" — a story that is already visible would not need to be uncovered.

• Option 2: "detectable" is incorrect because while something detectable could technically be found, it does not fit as naturally with "lay ... between the lines" as "invisible" does, and it shifts the intended emphasis from hiddenness to mere traceability.

• Option 3: "obvious" is incorrect for the same reason as "visible" — an obvious story would not require uncovering.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full sentence (and often the surrounding sentences) to identify the word that best fits both the grammar and the overall meaning/tone of the passage.

• Words like invisible, hidden, buried, obscured are common cloze-test choices when a text discusses "uncovering", "revealing", or "discovering" something.

Better still, I (2) ______ one of them tell it herself, with all her joys and doubts, her struggles and her triumphs, her heartbreaks, her achievements, the unique female way (3) ______ which she sees her world and her place in it. And who could be (4) ______ for this than Panchaali? It is her life, her voice, her questions, and her vision that I invite you (5) ______ 'The Palace of Illusions'.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. would have.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Better still, I would have one of them tell it herself, with all her joys and doubts..."

• Rule — "Would have" for a hypothetical/preferred wish: The construction "would have + object + base verb" (a causative structure) expresses a hypothetical preference or wish — here, the author's greater/preferred wish is for one of the women to narrate her own story herself.

• The word "Better still" signals an even more preferable alternative to what was just mentioned (uncovering the hidden story), reinforcing the conditional/hypothetical tone that fits "would have".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "could" is incorrect because it expresses mere ability/possibility, not the stronger hypothetical preference conveyed by "would have" in this reflective, wishful context.

• Option 3: "will" is incorrect because it denotes simple future certainty, which does not match the reflective, hypothetical tone established by "Better still".

• Option 4: "will have" is incorrect because it forms a future perfect construction that does not fit the hypothetical, wishful sense required here.

NOTE

• In cloze passages testing modals, pay close attention to signal words like "better still", "if only", "I wish" — they typically call for hypothetical modal forms such as would/would have, not simple future forms.

• Causative structure reminder: subject + would have + object + base verb (e.g., "I would have him explain it himself").

And who could be (4) ______ for this than Panchaali? It is her life, her voice, her questions, and her vision that I invite you (5) ______ 'The Palace of Illusions'.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...the unique female way in which she sees her world and her place in it."

• Rule — Preposition with relative clause "the way ... which": The standard, idiomatic construction is "the way in which", where the preposition "in" correctly links "way" to the relative clause describing how something is perceived or done.

• This is a fixed collocation frequently used in formal English to describe manner or perspective (e.g., "the way in which he handled the situation").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "though" is incorrect because it is a conjunction expressing contrast, which does not fit grammatically in this prepositional slot before "which".

• Option 2: "through" is incorrect because "the way through which" does not form a natural or idiomatic English collocation in this context.

• Option 3: "by" is incorrect because "the way by which" is grammatically possible in some contexts but does not fit as naturally or idiomatically with "sees her world" as "in which" does.

NOTE

• Common fixed prepositional collocations tested by SSC: "the way in which", "the manner in which", "the extent to which", "the reason for which/why".

• Always check whether the preposition preceding a relative pronoun (which/whom) forms a recognized fixed phrase in English.

I would uncover the story that lay (1) ______ between the lines of the men's exploits. Better still, I (2) ______ one of them tell it herself, with all her joys and doubts, her struggles and her triumphs, her heartbreaks, her achievements, the unique female way (3) ______ which she sees her world and her place in it. And who could be (4) ______ for this than Panchaali? It is her life, her voice, her questions, and her vision that I invite you (5) ______ 'The Palace of Illusions'.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. better suited.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "And who could be better suited for this than Panchaali?"

• Rule — "Suited for/to" collocation: The adjective "suited" idiomatically collocates with "for" (or "to"), meaning appropriate or fitting for a particular role or purpose. The comparative "better suited" means "more appropriate/fitting".

• The rhetorical question structure "who could be ___ for this than X?" expects a comparative adjective phrase describing suitability, which "better suited" precisely provides.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "better performed" is incorrect because "performed" does not collocate naturally with "for" in the sense of being an appropriate person for a role; "performed" describes an action being carried out, not a person's suitability.

• Option 3: "better meant" is incorrect because "meant for" describes something intended/designed for a purpose (usually objects), and does not fit naturally when describing a person's suitability to narrate her own story.

• Option 4: "best matched" is incorrect because it uses the superlative "best" (illogical in a two-way comparison introduced by "than") and "matched for" is not an idiomatic collocation.

NOTE

• Comparative structures with "than" (e.g., "better X than Y") require a comparative form ("better"), not a superlative ("best") — a common grammar trap in cloze passages.

• Common idiomatic pairing: "suited for/to a role/task/purpose".

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. into.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...that I invite you into 'The Palace of Illusions'."

• Rule — "Invite" + preposition: The verb "invite" idiomatically collocates with "into" when the object of invitation is a place, world, or experience one is being drawn or welcomed inside (here, the book/story "The Palace of Illusions" is metaphorically treated as a space the reader is invited to enter).

• The metaphor of a book as a "palace" one can be invited "into" reinforces why the preposition of entry/movement-within, "into", is the natural fit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "of" is incorrect because "invite you of" is not a grammatically valid collocation with "invite".

• Option 3: "upon" is incorrect because "invite you upon" is not an idiomatic English collocation.

• Option 4: "on to" is incorrect because while "invite onto" can occasionally be used for surfaces/platforms (e.g., "invite someone onto a stage"), it does not fit the metaphor of being welcomed inside a narrative "palace" as naturally as "into" does.

NOTE

• Common collocations with "invite": invite someone into a room/world/story, invite someone to a party/event, invite someone for dinner.

• Cloze passages testing prepositions often hinge on fixed verb-preposition collocations — memorising common ones (invite into/to/for, apply for/to, depend on, etc.) is essential for SSC exams.
